summary: This RFC specifies link and node routing metrics and constraints for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, for use by RPL. Unlike typical metrics based on hop counts or link costs, they reflect the constraints of LLNs.

plainLanguage.summary: Low-power networks have their own routing problems: a link may be good for a moment and useless later, and a router may be about to run out of battery. This RFC defines the measurements such a network can advertise and the rules for combining them along a path.

what node energy object in rpl
subtitle: What a low-power network measures when it chooses which way to send a packet.

tldr.problem: The routing protocols designed for wired networks measure links with simple static numbers such as a cost, which do not describe a network of battery-powered nodes whose links come and go.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of metric and constraint objects that RPL can carry in its messages: node energy, hop count, throughput, latency, link quality, expected transmissions and link colour, each with a common header that says how to combine the values along a path.
tldr.outcome: A low-power network can steer traffic around weak links, away from nodes that are nearly out of power, or towards links with a property the operator wants.

facts.label: ETX encoding
facts.value: The ETX value times 128, in 16 bits

today: RFC 6551 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it defines the metric and constraint objects used by RPL as specified in RFC 6550.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
Low-power and lossy networks have routing characteristics of their own, spelled out in RFC 5548, RFC 5673, RFC 5826 and RFC 5867. Historically, interior gateway protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS have used quantitative static link metrics. Other mechanisms, such as the MPLS traffic engineering extensions, make use of other link attributes, the available reserved bandwidth or link affinities, to compute constrained shortest paths.

This document specifies the routing metrics and constraints to be used in path calculation by RPL, the routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks specified in RFC 6550. One of its prime objectives is to define a flexible mechanism for advertising those metrics and constraints. Some RPL implementations may elect to adopt an extremely simple approach based on a single metric with no constraint, while others may use a larger set of link and node metrics and constraints, and new ones could be defined later as needed.

The metrics and constraints are carried in objects that are optional from the point of view of an RPL implementation, so implementations are free to include different subsets of the functions defined here. Specific sets of metrics and constraints and other optional RPL parameters for use in key environments are to be specified as compliance profiles in applicability profile documents from the ROLL working group. RPL can even make use of no metric at all, for example by using the Objective Function defined in RFC 6552.

RPL is a distance vector routing protocol variant that builds directed acyclic graphs based on routing metrics and constraints. The rules for forming the graph are defined in RFC 6550. The root of the graph may advertise a routing constraint used as a filter to prune links and nodes that do not satisfy specific properties: it may be required that a path traverses only mains-powered nodes, or only links with at least a minimum reliability, or only links with a specific colour reflecting a user-defined link characteristic such as the link layer supporting encryption.

A routing metric is a quantitative value used to evaluate the path cost. Link and node metrics are usually, but not always, additive. The best path is the one that satisfies all supplied constraints, if any, and that has the lowest cost with respect to some specified metrics. It is also called the shortest constrained path in the presence of constraints. Metrics can be categorised as link versus node metrics, qualitative versus quantitative, and dynamic versus static.

Some characteristics may be used either as constraints or as metrics, or sometimes both: a path may be computed to avoid links below a given reliability, or the path offering the most links above that reliability may be preferred. The use of metrics and constraints is not exclusive, so hop count can be advertised both as a metric to optimise on and as a constraint such as a limit on the number of hops.

Links in low-power networks commonly have rapidly changing characteristics, so metrics must be dynamic and the change must be smoothed out to avoid routing oscillations. Nodes' resources, such as residual energy, change continuously and may have to be taken into account during the path computation. The document is careful about the pace at which metric values change, because a routing metric that changes too often can cause instability. When a dynamic metric is used, the implementation should use a multi-threshold scheme rather than fine-grained updates reflecting each individual change, to avoid spurious and unnecessary routing changes, and the requirements on reporting frequency may differ among metrics, so different reporting rates may be used for each.

The metrics and constraints used by a deployment are signalled along the graph that is built according to the Objective Function, and they are advertised in the DODAG Information Object message of RFC 6550. RPL may be used to build graphs with different characteristics: one deployment may want to maximise reliability, another may use the energy node characteristic as a constraint so as to avoid battery-powered nodes while optimising link throughput. The specification of the Objective Functions is out of the scope of this document, which defines metrics and constraints that are decoupled from it, so a generic Objective Function can be used with any of them.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives a low-power network a menu of things it can measure and advertise, and leaves each implementation free to pick the ones that suit it. A constraint says which nodes and links a path is allowed to use, a metric says how good a path is, and the network picks the path that breaks no constraint and has the best metric.

sections.title: The Common Object Format
sections.content:
Routing metrics and constraints are carried within the DAG Metric Container object defined in RFC 6550. If several metrics or constraints are present in the container, an Objective Function can define how they are used to determine the best path. The Routing Metric and Constraint objects represent a metric or a constraint of a particular type, may appear in any order in the container, and have a common format consisting of one or more bytes with a common header.

The Routing Metric and Constraint Type field is 8 bits and uniquely identifies each object, and is managed by IANA. The Length field is 8 bits and gives the length of the object body in bytes, from 0 to 255. The Res Flags field is 16 bits, and its unassigned bits are reserved: they must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. Four bits of it are defined. The P flag is only used for recorded metrics: when cleared, all nodes along the path successfully recorded the metric, and when set, one or several nodes along the path could not record it, either from lack of knowledge or because policy prevented it. The C flag says whether the object refers to a routing constraint, when set, or a routing metric, when cleared. The O flag is used only for constraints: when set, the constraint is optional, and when cleared it is mandatory. The R flag is only relevant for a metric and says whether the metric is recorded along the path, when set, or aggregated, when cleared.

The A field is 3 bits and is only relevant for metrics. It says whether the aggregated metric is additive, reports a maximum, reports a minimum, or is multiplicative. It has no meaning when the C flag is set and is only valid when the R bit is cleared; otherwise it must be set to zero and ignored on receipt. The Prec field is 4 bits and gives the precedence of this object relative to the other objects in the container, which is useful when a container holds several metric objects. Its value runs from 0 to 15, and 0 means the highest precedence.

An object may also include one or more type-length-value data sets. Each has a 1-byte type, a 1-byte length giving the length of the value field in bytes from 0 to 255, and a variable value. Unrecognised TLVs must be silently ignored while still being propagated in the messages a receiving node generates. IANA manages the code points for all TLVs carried in these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Every measurement travels in the same kind of envelope. The envelope says what kind of measurement it is, how long the value is, whether it is a rule or a score, and how to combine the values from several nodes into one number for the path.

sections.title: How Several Objects Are Used Together
sections.content:
When the container holds a single aggregated metric, the order relation for choosing the best path is derived implicitly from the metric type: lower is better for hop count, link latency and ETX, while higher is better for node energy and throughput. The node energy metric, for example, is aggregated along paths with an explicit minimum function and the best path is selected through an implied maximum function, because the metric is energy.

When the container holds several aggregated metrics, they are used as tiebreakers according to the precedence given by their Prec field values. An example is hop count as the primary criterion, link quality level as the secondary and node energy as the ultimate tiebreaker, where the Prec fields bear strictly increasing values such as 0, 1 and 2. If several aggregated metrics happen to bear the same Prec value, the behaviour is implementation dependent.

Two further rules apply to the objects as a whole. Where more than one object of a specific type is received, the second object must be silently ignored. And in the presence of a constraint, a node must include a metric of the same type, which is used to check whether the constraint is met; in all cases a node must not change the content of the constraint.

Because the length of RPL options is encoded in one octet, they cannot exceed 255 bytes, and that applies to the container as well. In the vast majority of cases the advertised metrics and constraints do not need that much space, but there may be circumstances where more space is needed, for example when a set of metrics is recorded along a long path. In that case, to avoid overflow, the metrics are carried in multiple container objects, and for the rest of the document that use is treated as one long container.
sections.plainLanguage: With one measurement, the kind of measurement decides whether a bigger or a smaller number is better. With several, they are used in turn, in the order the precedence field gives, so the first one usually decides and the rest break ties. A rule about which nodes may be used always comes with a matching measurement so the rule can be checked.

sections.title: The Node Objects
sections.content:
The Node State and Attribute object provides information on node characteristics. It may be present in the container, and there must not be more than one of it as a constraint or as a metric per container. Its reserved flags must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt, and two flags are defined. The A flag is the data aggregation attribute: when set, the node can act as a traffic aggregator, which some applications may use to reduce the amount of traffic on the network and so increase its lifetime in battery-operated environments. The O flag says the node is overloaded and may not be able to process traffic, set for example on CPU overload or lack of memory; a simple one-bit flag gives enough granularity, similar to the overload bit used in protocols such as IS-IS, and it is recommended to avoid frequent changes of it to avoid routing oscillations.

The Node Energy object provides information related to node energy and may be used as a metric or as a constraint. Power and energy are critical resources in these networks, and there is no simple abstraction covering the range of power sources and storage devices used, which include mains-powered nodes, primary batteries, energy scavengers and secondary storage. Scavengers may provide a reliable low level of power, a reliable but periodic stream such as a well-placed solar cell, or unpredictable power. Routes viable when the sun is shining may disappear at night, and a pump turning on may connect two previously disconnected sections of a network.

Because of that complexity, the document defines two levels of fidelity. The simplest relies on a 2-bit field encoding three types of power source: powered, battery and scavenger. The mid-complexity solution is a single parameter that encodes the energetic happiness of battery-powered and scavenging nodes. For a scavenging node the quantity is the power provided by the scavenger divided by the power consumed by the application, in units of percent, so a node harvesting more than it consumes registers above 100. For a battery-powered device it is the expected lifetime divided by the desired minimum lifetime, also as a percentage. Two example calculations are given for the battery case, using either the measured power consumption against the desired maximum power, or the estimated energy left in the battery against the target energy remaining.

The sub-object carrying this information has three flags. The I bit is only relevant when the node type is used as a constraint and stipulates inclusion versus exclusion: when set, nodes of the type given in the node type field must be included, and when cleared they must be excluded. The T field is a 2-bit node type, where T=0 is a mains-powered node, T=1 a battery-powered node and T=2 a node powered by an energy scavenger. The E bit says the estimated percentage of remaining energy is present in the E_E field when set for a metric; when set for a constraint, the E_E field is a threshold for inclusion or exclusion. The E_E field itself is an 8-bit unsigned integer holding an estimated percentage of remaining energy, and it must be set to zero when the E flag is cleared. If the object has several sub-objects when used as a constraint, each one adds or subtracts node subsets as they are parsed in order, and the initial set is full if the first I bit is an exclusion and empty if it is an inclusion.

The Hop Count object reports the number of traversed nodes along the path. As a constraint, the root indicates the maximum number of hops a path may traverse, and when that number is reached no other node can join the path. As a metric, each visited node simply increments the hop count field, and the first node along a path inserting such a metric must set the field to 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The node objects describe the router itself rather than the link to its neighbour. One says whether the node can aggregate traffic and whether it is overloaded. One says how its power is supplied and how much is left. One counts the routers along the path.

sections.title: The Link Objects
sections.content:
Throughput. Many of these networks support a wide range of throughputs. For some links this is due to variable coding, and for the deeply duty-cycled links found in many networks the variability comes from trading power consumption for bit rate: several MAC layer protocols let the effective bit rate vary over more than three orders of magnitude with a corresponding change in power consumption. It may therefore be desirable for nodes to report the range of throughput their links can handle as well as the throughput currently available. The object is made of throughput sub-objects and must contain at least one, of which the first must be the most recently estimated actual throughput; how that estimate is made is outside the scope of the document. Each sub-object has a fixed length of 4 bytes, and the throughput is a 32-bit unsigned integer expressed in bytes per second.

Latency. The latency of many link layers can also vary over many orders of magnitude, again with a corresponding change in power consumption. Some link layers allow the latency to be adjusted globally on the subnet, link by link, or not at all; some insist it is fixed for a given link but allow it to vary from link to link. The object is made of latency sub-objects, at least one, each of a fixed length of 4 bytes, with the latency a 32-bit unsigned integer expressed in microseconds. It may be used as a constraint, for example that the latency must not exceed some value, or as an aggregated additive metric whose value is updated along the path.

Link reliability. In these networks link reliability can be degraded for reasons such as signal attenuation and interference, over time scales from milliseconds to days, often periodic and linked to human activity. Packet error rates can generally be measured directly and other metrics such as bit error rate are derived from them. A change in link quality can affect network connectivity, so link quality may be taken into account as a critical routing metric. Two reliability metrics are defined: the Link Quality Level and the ETX metric, and a deployment may use one, the other, or both.

The Link Quality Level object quantifies the link reliability with a discrete value from 0 to 7, where 0 means the quality is unknown and 1 is the highest quality; how it is computed is implementation specific. When used as a metric it can only be recorded, so each traversed node may record the quality of its incoming link, and a node can then select its parent by user-defined rules such as choosing the path with the most links reporting a value of 3 or less. Counters compress the information: for each value encountered, only the number of matching links is reported.

The ETX metric is the number of transmissions a node expects to make to a destination to deliver a packet successfully. Unlike the quality level, it provides a discrete value, which need not be an integer, computed by a formula: an implementation may use ETX = 1 / (Df * Dr), where Df is the measured probability that a packet is received by the neighbour and Dr the measured probability that the acknowledgement is received successfully. The document does not mandate a formula. The value is carried in 16 bits as the ETX multiplied by 128 and rounded to the nearest whole number, so an ETX of 3.569 becomes 457, and a value above 511.9921875 becomes the maximum of 65535. As a metric it can be aggregated additively along the path, each node adding the ETX of its own link to the path cost it received.

Link colour. The Link Color object is an administrative 10-bit link constraint, which may be static or dynamically adjusted, used to avoid or attract specific links for specific traffic types. A colour is a specific set of bit values, so the 10-bit field is a flag field rather than a scalar value; each node can then select its parent by rules such as choosing the path with the most links whose first bit is set, for example encrypted links. When used as a recorded metric, a counter compresses the information by reporting the number of links for each colour. When used as a constraint, the body holds sub-objects with an I bit that says whether links with that colour must be included or excluded. It is left to the implementer to define the meaning of each bit.
sections.plainLanguage: The link objects measure the connection itself: how much it can carry, how slow it is, how reliable it is, and what kind of link it is. Reliability comes in two forms: a simple grade from zero to seven, and the expected number of transmissions needed to get a packet through.

sections.title: Reporting Changing Values Without Breaking the Network
sections.content:
Dynamically calculated metrics are of the utmost importance in many circumstances, because a variety of metrics change frequently and the routing decisions have to adapt. Care must be given to the pace at which changes are reported: the attributes change according to their own time scales, and RPL controls the reporting rate.

To minimise metric updates, multi-threshold algorithms may be used to decide when updates should be sent. Where practical, low-pass filtering or hysteresis should be used to avoid rapid fluctuations of these values. The path computation algorithms themselves are out of the scope of the document, but it is recommended to design the route optimisation carefully to avoid computing new routes too often when metric values change.

Controlled adaptation of the metrics and of the rate at which paths are computed is critical to avoid undesirable routing instabilities, which result in increased latencies and packet loss because of temporary micro-loops. Excessive route changes also hurt traffic and power consumption in the network, and so can limit how far it scales.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the measurements keep moving, the document asks implementations to report changes in steps and to filter out short-lived blips. Reporting every tiny change would make the network keep rebuilding its routes, which costs power and can send traffic round in circles for a while.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Routing metrics should be handled in a secure and trustful manner. RPL should not allow a malicious node to falsely advertise that it has good metrics, so as to be selected as the preferred next-hop router for other nodes' traffic and intercept packets. Another attack may consist of making intermittent attacks on a link in an attempt to constantly modify the link quality and the associated routing metric, leading to potential fluctuation in the graph. It is therefore recommended that an RPL implementation put in place mechanisms to stop advertising routing metrics for highly unstable links that may be subject to attacks.

Some routing metrics may also be used to identify areas of weakness in the network, such as a highly unreliable link or a node running low on energy, and such information may be used by a potential attacker. It is recommended to consider carefully which metrics RPL uses and the level of visibility they give about the state of the network, or to use the appropriate security measures specified in RFC 6550 to protect that information. Since the routing metrics and constraints are carried within RPL messages, the security routing mechanisms defined in RFC 6550 apply here.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers a node advertises about itself are part of the routing, so they have to be protected. A node that lies about its quality could attract other nodes' traffic, and a node that keeps changing its reports could make the network keep rebuilding its routes. The document also warns that some measurements reveal where the weak spots are.

viz.caption: THE ROUTING METRIC AND CONSTRAINT OBJECT HEADER

fields.name: Routing-MC-Type
fields.desc: Identifies the metric or constraint type.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Unassigned bits, set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: A
fields.desc: How the aggregated value combines: additive, maximum, minimum or multiplicative.

fields.name: Prec
fields.desc: Precedence against the other objects in the container, where 0 is the highest.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length of the object body in bytes, from 0 to 255.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT ROUTING METRIC AND CONSTRAINT OBJECTS

cells: Node characteristics such as aggregation and overload
Remaining energy and the type of power source
Sub-objects with flags, node type and E_E
How much the link can carry
Link reliability on a scale of 0 to 7
Expected transmissions to deliver a packet
An administrative set of link flags
10 bits plus a counter or an include flag

viz.caption: THE FLAGS IN THE COMMON HEADER

items.title: C flag
items.text: Set when the object is a constraint, cleared when it is a metric.

items.title: O flag
items.text: Set when the constraint is optional rather than mandatory.

items.title: R flag
items.text: Set when the metric is recorded along the path, cleared when it is aggregated.

items.title: P flag
items.text: Set when some node along the path could not record the metric.

items.title: A field
items.text: Whether the aggregated metric is additive, reports a maximum or a minimum, or is multiplicative.

items.title: Prec field
items.text: The precedence against the other objects in the container, where 0 is the highest.

viz.caption: FORMULAS THE METRICS MAY USE, FROM RFC 6551

data.title: Example formulas
data.code:
ETX = 1 / (Df * Dr)

E_E = P_in / P_out                  (scavenging nodes)
E_E = expected lifetime / desired minimum lifetime   (battery nodes)
